7	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.

21	2. Specify the problem along four dimensions, each as IS versus IS NOT:

23	   - WHERE: in which locations, processes, teams or channels is it observed, and where is it not?
24	   - WHEN: when was it first observed, when since, under what conditions or cycle, and when not?
25	   - EXTENT: how many, how much, what trend, what share - and what is not affected?
26	3. For each IS/IS NOT pair, list distinctions: what is true of the IS that is not true of the IS NOT.

45	CASE OD2-DEV-OBVWRONG: Larkmoor Parks: the maintenance overtime overrun
46	
47	Setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
48	
49	Presenting request: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.
50	
51	INITIAL EVIDENCE
52	E1 [stage S1] Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director (financial-record): Re: Overtime variance, April–September. Parks maintenance overtime for April–September totals $688,400, compared with $412,100 for the same months last year (+67%) and a budget of $430,000. Council's Finance Committee has asked for an explanation and corrective plan by 15 December. For reference, this year's adopted reductions for the department were: citywide hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions (from 6 January); deferral of two mower replacements ($118,000); non-renewal of the after-hours closing services contract ($96,000); reduced seasonal temp hours ($40,000). Please route your response through this office.
53	E2 [stage S1] Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November (leadership-account): 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. We started the year six maintenance workers short and we're at seventeen now. Every vacancy is a route somebody has to cover after their shift. July was brutal too, because the heat meant extra irrigation checks and mowing catch-up. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' Asked about other drivers, she said the closing contract 'was a small line, crews absorbed it.' She said she had not seen a breakdown of overtime by pay code.
54	E3 [stage S1] HR/payroll extract prepared at the Director's request (system-record): Maintenance division, current year. Month: vacant maintenance-worker positions (of 112) / overtime paid. Jan 6 / $52.3k; Feb 8 / $49.1k; Mar 10 / $55.0k; Apr 12 / $104.2k; May 15 / $109.0k; Jun 17 / $118.1k; Jul 17 / $121.4k; Aug 17 / $119.3k; Sep 17 / $116.4k. HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'
55	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November (staff-account): 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.
56	E5 [stage S1] City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611 (log): Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. They're each pulling an extra grand a month.' Caller declined follow-up contact. Status: referred to Internal Audit for review on 26 August.
57	E6 [stage S1] Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November (staff-account): Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.
58	E7 [stage S1] Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance (system-record): Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.

65	X5 [stage S1] Budget office overtime workbook by pay code and district, April–September, current and prior year - source: Office of Budget & Management, payroll analytics (financial-record) - file: evidence/X5.txt
66	X6 [stage S1] Recreation division event permit summary, April–September - source: Recreation permit system (system-record) - file: evidence/X6.txt
67	X7 [stage S1] City Manager hiring-freeze directive and citywide exemption log - source: City Manager's Office (document) - file: evidence/X7.txt
68	X8 [stage S1] Regional parks benchmarking survey: overtime share of maintenance payroll, prior fiscal year - source: Regional municipal parks association (external-data) - file: evidence/X8.txt
69	X9 [stage S1] Collective agreement excerpts, Articles 12 and 14 (overtime and call-back) - source: City–Local 418 collective agreement (document) - file: evidence/X9.txt
70	X10 [stage S1] Internal Audit memo on hotline intake #2611 - source: Internal Audit memo IA-26-31, 30 October (prior-report) - file: evidence/X10.txt
71	X11 [stage S1] Workers' compensation claim log, parks maintenance, April–September - source: Risk Management claims system (system-record) - file: evidence/X11.txt
72	X12 [stage S1] Fleet maintenance log for parks mowers and utility vehicles, January–September - source: City Fleet Services (log) - file: evidence/X12.txt

74	CANDIDATE HYPOTHESES
75	H1: The overtime increase is driven mainly by maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze, with crews working extra hours to cover open routes.
76	H2: The overtime increase is driven mainly by nightly closing duties moved onto maintenance staff as 3-hour-minimum call-backs after the after-hours closing contract was not renewed.
77	H3: Padded or fictitious call-back claims account for a material share of the overtime increase.
78	H4: Extra irrigation and mowing work caused by the hot summer is a main driver of the overtime increase.
79	H5: In Eastgate, the supervisor is steering lock-up call-backs to a favored subset of staff.
80

82	R1: Rise in maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze -> Rise in maintenance overtime spending, April–September (causes)
83	R2: Non-renewal of the after-hours closing contract for Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook -> Rise in call-back overtime in those three districts (causes)
84	R3: Higher overtime hours among maintenance staff -> Rise in workers' compensation injury claims (causes)

87	A1: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.
88	A2: Impose an immediate department-wide cap of 12 overtime hours per worker per month.
89	A3: Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.
90	A4: Remove the Eastgate supervisor from call-back scheduling and issue her a written reprimand for favoritism.

input.brief:
The overrun is mainly a side effect of not renewing the closing contract, not of the hiring freeze. From 1 April, nightly closing at 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook moved to maintenance staff as call-backs. Each call-back is paid at a 3-hour minimum, even though a closing round takes 30–45 minutes. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. 1,962 of 2,295 call-backs carry the CLOSE code, and none are in Summit Hill, which kept its contract. Holdover overtime, the type vacancies would drive, rose only about 5%, and most of that is the July wage increase. Summit Hill has vacancies but almost no rise. The contract saved $96k, and the call-backs cost about $250k more.

Internal Audit checked the fraud allegation against lock logs and found no padding. Eastgate favoritism is plausible, since the same few people sign up and the sheets were discarded, but it is unproven. The link between overtime and injuries is only an association, because hours worked by the injured staff were never checked.

I'm fairly confident in this. Restore contracted closing, or re-tender it, and track call-back spending. Don't cap overtime, discipline the two employees, or discipline the supervisor. Keep the sign-up sheets from now on. Review the Eastgate assignments, and match injury claims to payroll hours. The eleven-position exemption is not justified by this evidence.
